Chapter 2: Learning from Mentors and the Power of Influence
If you think back on your own creative journey, chances are, there are people who’ve left a mark—mentors, friends, maybe even a few rivals.
In those early days making music in New York, relationships like these were just as meaningful as any song, any stage, or any wild night in a smoky club. The folk scene was teeming with unique personalities, each one bringing their own story—and a whole new way of looking at music.
One of the most surprising lessons? The value of just listening. Imagine sitting at the back of a dimly lit club, soaking in the sound of someone who’s been playing longer than you’ve been alive. Their songs don’t just entertain—they carry the weight of years, of lived experience. And when you watch them command a room, you realize... mastery isn’t just about perfect technique. It’s about connecting, about making every word and every note count.
Some of the best lessons come out of nowhere. Maybe it’s a random conversation with an older musician in a packed bar—something small that flips the way you approach a song. Mentors aren’t always handing out advice directly, either. Sometimes, it’s their attitude, their willingness to take risks, that leaves the deepest impression. They show you that it’s possible to be serious about your craft while still staying open to new ideas and a little bit of experimentation.
And then, there’s humility. The folk scene could get competitive, and not every night was a triumph. Sometimes the crowd just isn’t feeling it, or a new arrangement falls flat. Those moments? They really test you. It’s tempting to play it safe, but the musicians who last are the ones who keep pushing, who see those stumbles as a part of the process.
Influence doesn’t just come from other musicians, either. Books, paintings, films—they all offer fresh ways to think about creativity. Reading a poet or getting lost in a novel, you start to see that storytelling sits at the heart of every great song. The real challenge? Turning that sense of narrative into music—writing songs that feel both deeply personal and somehow universal.
Collaboration plays a huge role, too. Working with other musicians brings new energy and perspectives. Sometimes it’s as simple as learning a new chord or exploring a different style. Other times, it’s about listening—really listening—and responding in real time. The best moments feel effortless, almost as if the music is writing itself.
Of course, there are always moments of doubt. The pressure to stand out, to make it in a crowded scene, can feel overwhelming. It’s easy to look around and think you’re falling behind, or that success is always just out of reach. But then, the words of mentors and friends echo back, reminding you that every artist’s journey is their own. What really matters is just keeping at it, one day at a time.
In the end, it’s clear how much those relationships shape us. The lessons from mentors and peers don’t just influence the music—they shape the way we see art, and even life itself. Sure, the path is still full of unknowns. But it’s also packed with possibility. In a city that’s always changing, every day offers a new chance to learn, to grow, and to create something meaningful.
